view.title: Social Media Content
view.dek: This edition reviews Instagram content only. What the six providers published on their official Instagram accounts between 25 July and 22 October 2026, read after the window closed. The posts are kept apart from the website evidence, which was captured on 23 October 2026 and has its own dates.

review_flag: This view is shown on the staging draft for editorial review. Editorial approval has not been recorded, and the release build stays blocked until the owner records it.
scope: The official company Instagram accounts of the providers: four Canadian accounts (Venn, Float, Loop, Keep) and Airwallex's global account, plus @tryramp, supplied by the owner as Ramp's global account. No official Ramp source links @tryramp, so its provider attribution is unresolved. No founder, employee, partner or reseller accounts, and no other social network.

51 records published in the window: 32 attributed posts (Venn 9, Airwallex 23) and 19 records on @tryramp with unresolved provider attribution. Findings about providers use the 32 attributed posts; the 19 @tryramp records are listed and labelled, and no conclusion about Ramp rests on them.
Posts published 25 July to 22 October 2026 inclusive, by their Toronto publication date (90 days). Each date comes from the post page's own timestamp.

26 October 2026, after the window closed: Float, Loop and Keep from 9:01 to 9:09 p.m., then Venn, @tryramp and Airwallex, with post records from 9:45 to 10:15 p.m. Toronto time. The browser was signed in to Instagram; nothing was followed, liked or commented on.
Every grid and Reels post that the account showed within the window at collection time, subject to the limits in each row below. A post deleted or hidden before 26 October would not be seen.

33 of the 51 records are reels: for these, the cover frame, caption and header only. No video was played, so nothing here describes what a video says or shows after its cover. Nine carousels were read slide by slide; one, on @tryramp, was only partly captured and is not used as an example.

Reposts (Instagram does not show when a repost was made), Stories, highlights, live videos, the Tagged tab, ads and the @tryvault account. Displayed likes, comments and views were recorded with their read times but are not shown or compared: posts had different ages, and a collaboration's counts include another account's audience.
coverage_dek: One row per provider, in the page's usual order: 51 records in all, 32 attributed posts and 19 @tryramp records with unresolved provider attribution. A count of 0 means no in-window post was found on the surfaces reviewed; it says nothing about whether the provider is active elsewhere.
patterns_dek: These observations describe this sample: the 32 attributed posts from Venn and Airwallex in one 90-day window, read from covers and captions, with the 19 @tryramp records mentioned only where labelled. They do not show what the providers intend or what the posts achieved.

patterns.title: Venn's posts were mostly customer stories
patterns.body: Six of Venn's nine posts tell a customer's story, about three customers: Spellbook (three posts), Queen's Commerce Society (two) and one other business. Two give customer figures in the caption, such as $25,000 saved in a year, and $1,300 in transaction fees and $1,000 in FX fees saved. The captions attribute the figures to the customer and do not say how they were calculated, which matches the website pattern "Figures often appeared without their basis".
patterns.denominator: Venn: 9 posts, all published by @venn.ca; 7 reels read from cover and caption, 1 image, 1 carousel read slide by slide.

patterns.title: Rates, fees and eligibility rarely appeared
patterns.body: Two of the 32 attributed posts state a product rate, both from Venn: 1% cashback in a customer story, and an interest promotion of up to 3.50% with its main condition in the same caption. One more reports a customer's fee savings. No attributed post states an FX fee, a plan price or who can apply for a card. On the websites, these were the main subjects of the three findings.
patterns.denominator: 32 attributed posts (Venn 9, Airwallex 23), captions and covers only for reels. A reel could state terms in its video; that was not checked. The 19 @tryramp records are not counted here.

patterns.title: Airwallex's account carried sponsorships, events and company life
patterns.body: Of Airwallex's 23 posts, 14 cover sport sponsorships, events, podcasts and other media, and 6 cover the company, its staff and its own events. Three address a product or programme directly: a creator post about the corporate card, a case study about Arsenal's payments, and a call for nominations to Startup Finance 30. None is about Canada.
patterns.denominator: Airwallex: 23 posts on a global account, 18 published by @airwallex and 5 collaborations.

patterns.title: Collaborations were common on @airwallex and @tryramp
patterns.body: On @airwallex, 5 of 23 posts are collaborations; 4 carry a paid-partnership label, 3 in the header and 1 in the caption only. On @tryramp, whose provider attribution is unresolved, 15 of the 19 records are collaborations, 13 of them published by other accounts, and 4 carry Instagram's "Paid partnership with tryramp" label. These @tryramp figures describe the account, not Ramp.
patterns.denominator: 23 attributed Airwallex posts and, separately, 19 @tryramp records with unresolved provider attribution; the two are not added together. Labels as shown; nothing here says what was paid or to whom.

patterns.title: Three Canadian accounts had no posts in the window
patterns.body: Float's newest post was dated 5 June 2026, Loop's 11 June 2026 and Keep's 17 July 2024. Of the four Canadian accounts, only Venn published in the window.
patterns.denominator: 4 Canadian accounts; grid and Reels surfaces reviewed (Keep's profile shows no Reels tab).

selection: Four posts, each showing a different way of presenting an offer or a next step, chosen for what they show about how a claim travels to Instagram: two from Venn and two from Airwallex. They are not ranked and were not chosen by displayed counts. The 19 @tryramp records are not used as examples while their provider attribution is unresolved. For reels, only the cover and caption were reviewed, so each reading is limited to those.

examples.approach: Customer story with a feature list
examples.title: A customer story that repeats the cashback rate

shows.q: You know a tool is working when the team can't imagine running without it.

shows: It then reports that a customer's general manager, after more than a year on Venn, was asked which features have become non-negotiable, and lists four. The last is

shows.q: 1% cashback that arrives in the account every month automatically

shows: . The caption names no plan, monthly spend limit or other condition for the rate.
website: Venn's pricing footnote, captured on 23 October 2026, limits cashback to card spend on the first $5,000 a month on Essentials and the first $25,000 on Plus, while its cards page says there are no tiers, thresholds or caps (
). Those are October terms. Whether any plan limit applied on 30 July 2026, when this post was published, was not established.
examples.reading: The caption gives the rate without naming a plan. I cannot say it left out a condition that applied at the time: Venn's plan limits were captured in October, and whether they applied on 30 July was not established. What the post does show is a rate repeated in a customer story with no plan beside it, so a reader cannot tell from the caption which plans the rate covers.
examples.take: When a rate is repeated in a customer story, the plan it applies to can drop out of the caption. Hypothesis: naming the plan that earns the rate in posts that repeat it reduces rewards questions after sign-up. Measure rewards questions per new account in the first 60 days, for posts with and without the plan line.
examples.no_image_reason: The cover frame shows a person from behind and does not show the rate; the caption excerpt carries the point.

examples.title: A promotion that keeps the rate and its condition together

shows.q: Want to see exactly how much your cash is earning?

shows: and announces Venn's Interest Boost with a tracking banner that shows

shows.q: how much of your cash is earning the boosted rate (up to 3.50%) versus the standard rate

shows: . In the same caption it says the boost

shows.q: applies to funds added above your pre-promo average monthly

shows: balance; the capture cuts the sentence off before its last word.
website: , where Venn's cashback condition sat on a different page from the rate. This post is about a different offer, so it does not settle that finding.
examples.reading: Here the condition sits in the caption with the rate, the arrangement that test 1 proposes for card pages. The tracker the post describes also answers the reader's next question, how much of the balance qualifies. I did not watch the video, so I cannot say whether the video states the condition too.
examples.take: A promotional rate and its main condition fit in one caption. Hypothesis: a post that states both draws fewer "does my balance qualify?" questions than one that states the rate alone. Measure promotion questions per account opened through the post's link, against a rate-only version.
examples.no_image_reason: The cover frame is a small dashboard image with an account name blurred by the collector; it does not show the rate or the condition, so the caption excerpt is used instead.

examples.title: A creator post labelled as a paid partnership
shows: Published by the creator @thejoshvfx with @airwallex as collaborator; the header shows Instagram's "Paid partnership" label. The caption says

shows.q: Managing my biz spend from anywhere is unmatched with @airwallex

shows: , then invites comments. The caption names no market, plan, fee or condition, and the cover, which shows the creator at Oracle Park in San Francisco holding a card, shows none. The video was not watched, so whether it states any is not known.
website: Airwallex's Canadian card pages state a 1% cashback rate, with conditions on the pricing page (
). This post is on the global account; its caption and cover do not show whether the card or its terms apply in Canada.
examples.reading: In the caption and cover, the benefit is in the creator's words and no condition or market appears beside it; I did not watch the video, so I cannot say whether the video adds either. The disclosure is Instagram's label rather than a line in the caption. A reader outside the US cannot tell from the caption or cover where the card is offered.
examples.take: A creator caption can carry a benefit with no condition or market beside it. Question for your team: does each creator brief name the market served and the one condition a viewer most needs, in the caption as well as the video? Measure the share of enquiries from creator links that come from markets you serve.

examples.approach: Call to action with eligibility and a deadline
examples.title: A call to action that says who qualifies and by when
shows: All five slides were reviewed: a Startup Finance 30 cover with four judges, then one slide per judge. The caption names the judges and their companies, says the 30 will be chosen

shows.q: Nominations are now open until 13 September 2026
If you lead finance at a venture-backed startup

shows: , and ends with a web address.
website: : few first screens on the websites said who can apply or what happens next. This post is a nomination programme, not a product application, so it shows a way of writing eligibility, not how Airwallex presents card eligibility.
examples.reading: In one caption a reader learns who the programme is for, when it closes, who decides and where to go. Those are the questions finding 3 found most first screens left open, here for a much simpler offer.
examples.take: Question for your team: does each post that asks for a sign-up say who qualifies and the deadline before the link? Hypothesis: stating both raises the share of link clicks that become completed entries. Measure completed entries per link click, against a version without the eligibility line.

tests_note: The Instagram evidence does not replace any of the three tests. Two Venn posts bear on

: one repeats a rate without naming a plan (whether the October plan limits applied when it was published was not established), and one keeps a rate and its condition together. One Airwallex post bears on
. None is a stronger basis than the website pages: the posts are a different surface, published on different dates, and the reels were read from cover and caption only.
tests_decision: Three tests unchanged (27 October 2026). Reason: no social observation gives stronger evidence than the website observations behind tests 1 to 3; the posts that bear on them are consistent with those tests and are linked from this view.
